message.content:
Below is a concise “cheat‑sheet” of the most useful properties of hydrogen (the element H, atomic number 1).  
I’ve grouped them into **physical**, **chemical**, and **isotopic** categories so you can find what you need quickly.

| Property | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Symbol** | H | |
| **Atomic number** | 1 | |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 g mol⁻¹ | Weighted average of natural isotopes |
| **Electronic configuration** | 1s¹ | |
| **Pauling electronegativity** | 2.20 | |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | |
| **Electron affinity** | 0.754 eV (−72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) | |
| **Standard enthalpy of formation** | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) | |
| **Standard Gibbs free energy of formation** | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ | |
| **Standard molar entropy** | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | |
| **Standard molar heat capacity (298 K)** | 28.84 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.44 K) | |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | |
| **Density at STP (0 °C, 1 atm)** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ | |
| **Molar volume at STP** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | |
| **Dipole moment** | 0 D (non‑polar) | |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | |
| **Molecular weight of H₂** | 2.01588 g mol⁻¹ | |
| **Molecular weight of H₂O** | 18.01528 g mol⁻¹ | |
| **Typical uses** | Fuel (hydrogen combustion, fuel cells), ammonia synthesis (Haber process), petroleum refining, metal reduction, cryogenic cooling, etc. | |

### Isotopes

| Isotope | Symbol | Mass | Natural abundance | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Protium | ¹H | 1.007825 u | ~99.98 % | Most common; single proton nucleus |
| Deuterium | ²H (D) | 2.014102 u | ~0.02 % | One proton + one neutron; heavy water (D₂O) |
| Tritium | ³H (T) | 3.016049 u | <10⁻⁵ % | Radioactive (β⁻ emitter, half‑life 12.32 y); used in nuclear fusion research |

---

#### Quick‑reference cheat‑sheet (tab‑style)

```
H   | 1 | 1.008 | 1s¹ | 2.20 | 13.60 eV | 0.75 eV | 0 kJ/mol | 0 kJ/mol | 130.7 J/K | 28.8 J/K | –252.9 °C | –259.2 °C | 0.0899 g/L | 22.4 L/mol
```

Feel free to copy this table into your notes or spreadsheet. If you need more detailed data (e.g., temperature‑dependent thermodynamic functions, spectroscopic constants, or reaction kinetics), let me know!
